did_you_know.text: Did you know? Proverbs 25 opens by noting that these are Solomon’s proverbs, copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah.
Did you know? The chapter distinguishes between the glory of God, shown in concealing a matter, and the glory of kings, shown in investigating and clarifying it.
Did you know? The refining of silver serves as a metaphor for removing wickedness: just as impurities are removed to make a clean vessel, so wickedness must be removed to make way for righteous rule.
Did you know? The chapter encourages humility regarding status: it is better to wait until you are invited to come forward than to take an important place and then be asked to step down in disgrace.
Did you know? Words spoken at the right time and in the right way are compared to apples of gold in settings of silver—a picture of the beauty and value of appropriate speech.

Did you know? A faithful messenger is compared to the coolness of snow on a harvest day: he refreshes those who sent him and renews their spirits, unlike someone who disappoints the trust placed in him.
Did you know? The chapter teaches that patience and gentle speech can influence even a person in authority: “By patience” a ruler may be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break strong resistance.
Did you know? Even visits with friends require moderation: visiting too often may cause a friend to grow tired of your presence and even come to hate it.
Did you know? The command to feed a hungry enemy and give drink to a thirsty one teaches that the duty to show kindness is not limited to relationships with loved ones and friends.
Did you know? A person who lacks self-control is compared to a city broken into and left without walls—a metaphor emphasizing that losing self-control leaves a person exposed and defenseless.
